entry.title: “It looks mild to me”: How neuropathologists assess neurodegenerative disease

link.title: “It looks mild to me”: How neuropathologists assess neurodegenerative disease

entry.content:
Learning to see pathology

Humans have evolved a remarkable ability to recognize objects despite substantial variations in their appearance [1]. We can recognize a familiar object regardless of its orientation, size, color, or lighting conditions, often without even realizing how complex this task is.

However, recognizing objects is still a skill that needs to be developed. At the beginning, you simply do not see certain structures in the brain. Someone points them out to you, and you wonder how they managed to find them in the first place. After looking at similar slides for many consecutive days, you suddenly start detecting things that previously looked like nothing more than noise.

With experience, we also become better at applying previously acquired knowledge to unfamiliar structures and learning to recognize new types of pathology.

But why is recognizing pathological structures so difficult in the first place?

Why no two slides look the same

There are numerous sources of variability in histological images, some biological and others introduced during tissue preparation. I will discuss many of them in more detail in separate posts, but for now, here is a brief overview [2].

  1. Staining variability. Some slides will be stained more strongly than others. This applies both to the structures of interest and to the surrounding tissue. Differences in staining intensity, nonspecific background staining, and variations in color can substantially change the appearance of a slide.

  2. Tissue preservation. The postmortem interval (PMI), the time between death and tissue preservation, storage conditions, type of fixative, and duration of fixation can all influence tissue appearance and the detection of pathological structures.

  3. Anatomical variability and sectioning. No two tissue sections look exactly the same, even if they originate from the same anatomical region. This is partly due to natural anatomical differences between individuals and partly due to differences in the position and orientation of tissue sectioning.

  4. Artifacts. Stain deposits, tissue folds, tears, dirt, air bubbles, and imaging artifacts can all interfere with the assessment of pathology. Many of these artifacts we humans quickly learn to recognize and ignore, whereas computers may happily interpret them as objects of interest.

  5. Neurodegeneration. Degenerating tissue can lose some of the characteristics and anatomical landmarks that help us identify brain regions and cellular structures. Ironically, the tissue we are most interested in studying can also be the most difficult to recognize.

  6. Antibody variability. Different antibodies targeting the same protein can produce substantially different staining patterns. They may recognize different parts of the protein, different post-translational modifications, or different molecular forms.

  7. Biological variability. Even within a single brain region, pathology is rarely distributed uniformly. Certain cortical layers, cell populations, or tissue compartments may be particularly vulnerable, while neighboring structures remain relatively unaffected.

Many of these problems are common to medical pathology and histology in general. However, I would argue that some of them are particularly pronounced in neuropathology due to the remarkable structural and cellular heterogeneity of the brain.

It can take years to reliably distinguish signal from noise across different types of tissue and pathology. This is one of the reasons why neuropathological expertise is so valuable. What makes translating this expertise into computational methods particularly challenging is that much of this knowledge is acquired through experience. Written guidelines cannot always capture all the exceptions and nuances that an experienced neuropathologist encounters in everyday practice.

And if every image is slightly different and there seem to be more exceptions than rules, how do we develop a robust automated detection pipeline?

Before we get to computers, however, let us look at what we are actually trying to detect and how neuropathologists have traditionally assessed it.

What are we looking for?

In short, neuropathologists are looking for signs of disease. In the context of neurodegenerative diseases, we can broadly distinguish three categories of pathological changes.

Neurodegeneration and glial responses

Two particularly interesting aspects of neurodegenerative diseases are the extent of tissue damage and the associated glial responses. These include neuronal loss, changes in tissue architecture, white matter degeneration, and reactive changes in astrocytes and microglia.

Many of these changes can be identified using conventional histological stains, such as hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) or Nissl staining. More specialized staining methods, including immunohistochemistry (IHC), can help visualize specific changes, such as astrocyte reactivity, microglial activation, or myelin loss.

Pathological protein aggregates

One of the characteristic features of many neurodegenerative diseases is, of course, the abnormal accumulation of proteins or peptides. Examples include amyloid-β, phosphorylated tau, α-synuclein, TDP-43, FUS, and prion protein, among others.

Although the relationship between protein accumulation, neuronal death, and clinical symptoms is complex, these aggregates provide some of the most valuable neuropathological markers of neurodegenerative diseases. They are usually visualized using specialized staining methods, such as immunohistochemistry or silver staining (although you can sometimes spot plaques in H&E!).

Vascular pathology

Another major category of abnormalities includes changes affecting the brain’s blood vessels and blood supply. These include hemorrhages, infarcts (areas of tissue damage caused by insufficient blood supply), structural abnormalities of vessel walls, and the accumulation of proteins within vessel walls.

Some of these changes are visible during macroscopic examination, while others can be identified using conventional histological stains or more specialized staining methods. Vascular pathology frequently coexists with neurodegenerative pathology and can independently contribute to cognitive impairment [3].

Of course, this is a simplified classification, and these categories are not mutually exclusive. Other neuropathological findings include Hirano bodies, corpora amylacea, granulovacuolar degeneration, and tissue calcifications. Other disease processes, such as infections or tumors, may also coexist with neurodegenerative changes.

Pathology has been identified. What now?

When characterizing pathological changes, there are generally three questions of interest:

  • What are they? What morphological changes are present in the tissue? Which proteins accumulate, and in what molecular forms?
  • How much is there? Are there just a few pathological structures, or is the entire region severely affected? To what extent are cells and tissue structures damaged?
  • Where are they? Which brain regions are affected? Is the pathology in gray or white matter? Is it intracellular or extracellular? Does it affect neurons, glial cells, or blood vessels?

One approach is simply to describe the observed changes. Written reports remain one of the most important documents produced by neuropathologists. However, free-text descriptions can vary between neuropathologists, and transforming them into standardized data suitable for large-scale research is not always straightforward.

Several approaches are used to systematically describe and measure neuropathological changes. Let us go through them one by one.

It looks mild to me

The simplest approach is to establish whether pathology is present or absent. This is known as a binary assessment. Depending on the pathology and the criteria being used, a minimum number of lesions may be required to classify a region as positive.

However, knowing that something is present does not necessarily tell us much about its abundance. To overcome this limitation, neuropathologists frequently perform a semiquantitative assessment, assigning pathology to categories such as:

  • None (0)
  • Mild (1)
  • Moderate (2)
  • Severe (3)

Depending on the pathology and the guidelines being followed, additional categories or different terminology may be used.

But what exactly does moderate mean?

In many situations, the assessment relies on a combination of established criteria, visual reference examples, and previous experience. Essentially, does it look mild, moderate, or severe to you, considering all the examples of this particular pathology that you have previously encountered?

This is not necessarily a bad approach. Experienced neuropathologists can integrate a remarkable amount of visual and biological information into a relatively quick assessment. However, communicating and reproducing that assessment is not always straightforward.

What exactly does moderate plaque density mean?

Let us consider one of the best-known examples of semiquantitative assessment in neuropathology: the criteria developed by the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer’s Disease (CERAD). Published in 1991, these guidelines aimed to standardize the neuropathological assessment of Alzheimer’s disease and included reference images illustrating different densities of neuritic plaques [5], which I have tried to represent schematically below.

The approach makes intuitive sense: neuropathologists compare the observed pathology with reference images and assign the most appropriate category. However, things become more complicated when we consider the spatial variability of pathology.

The three microscopy images above give quite different impressions of plaque density. The catch? All three originate from the same tissue section.

Which image best represents the severity of pathology in this region? Should the assessment reflect the average plaque density, the most severely affected area, or an area considered representative?

The CERAD criteria focus on the areas of highest neuritic plaque density in the neocortex. However, identifying these areas, recognizing neuritic plaques, and estimating their density can still introduce variability between observers. CERAD investigators themselves addressed interlaboratory variability in 1994 [6].

Can we assume that everyone has interpreted these guidelines in exactly the same way over the past few decades? Probably not.

This is particularly important when comparing or combining neuropathological data from different laboratories.

Where rather than how much: neuropathological staging

Another commonly used approach to neuropathological assessment is staging.

Many neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by relatively stereotypical patterns of anatomical involvement, with pathology thought to appear in certain brain regions earlier than in others. Rather than measuring exactly how much pathology is present in each brain region, staging uses information about its anatomical distribution to estimate how far the pathological process has progressed.

Examples include:

  • Thal phases of amyloid-β deposition [7].
  • Braak stages of neurofibrillary tau pathology in Alzheimer’s disease [8].
  • Braak stages of Lewy pathology in Parkinson’s disease [9].
  • Staging of tau pathology in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) [10].
  • Staging of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) [11].
  • Staging of limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathological change (LATE-NC) [12].

Several of these staging systems are important components of contemporary neuropathological diagnostic criteria. They also provide a relatively time-efficient way of assessing pathology. Rather than examining every brain region, neuropathologists can examine a selection of regions that are informative about different stages of the pathological process.

Some protocols even recommend a stepwise approach: if pathology is absent from selected screening regions, additional staining may not be necessary [13].

This is a very practical approach, although it comes with limitations. Staging systems are largely based on observations across different individuals rather than direct observations of pathological progression within the same individual. Moreover, two individuals assigned to the same stage can differ substantially in the amount of pathology present in individual brain regions.

And, of course, there are always cases that refuse to fit neatly into our classification systems.

Can we simply count everything?

An alternative to assigning pathology to broad categories is manual counting. For example, pathological inclusions can be counted, and their density expressed as the number of inclusions per square millimeter of tissue.

Interestingly, the 2012 National Institute on Aging–Alzheimer’s Association (NIA-AA) guidelines for the neuropathological assessment of Alzheimer’s disease provide numerical examples of neuritic plaque densities corresponding to different CERAD categories [13]. This provides a more explicit reference for interpreting the categories, although the final CERAD score remains semiquantitative.

However, manually counting pathological structures across large tissue sections and multiple brain regions is extremely time-consuming. Things become even more complicated when the objective is to estimate the number of objects in three-dimensional tissue rather than simply count their profiles in two-dimensional sections.

For this, researchers can use stereological methods. Design-based stereology uses systematic random sampling and predefined counting rules to obtain unbiased estimates of properties such as the total number of neurons within a brain region.

Although extremely valuable, these methods require time, expertise, and appropriate tissue sampling. This makes their application to routine neuropathological assessments and large retrospective studies difficult and, in some cases, impossible with the available tissue or staining techniques.

Can computers help us?

Binary assessments, semiquantitative scores, and staging systems have served neuropathologists well for decades. They allow experienced neuropathologists to extract diagnostically relevant information from complex biological tissue within a reasonable amount of time.

However, the measurements that are sufficient to establish a diagnosis are not necessarily sufficient to answer our research questions.

Between none and severe, there is an enormous amount of biological information that we are currently not capturing. Ideally, we would like to know not only how much pathology is present, but also what these pathological structures look like, where exactly they are located, which cells are affected, and how they relate to other pathological changes.

We would also like to assess these changes across many more brain regions and individuals than is practically possible with manual approaches.

Could computers help us extract this information without spending the next few decades counting pathological inclusions under a microscope?

This is where computational neuropathology comes into play, and where things start to get particularly interesting.

Useful resources

  • The Cell Image Library — A publicly accessible repository of microscopy images, including the brain tissue images used in this post. You can download and explore whole-slide images from Alzheimer’s disease cases! Simply download the submitted data (beware, the files are large!) and open the images in QuPath, a free, open-source software for digital pathology.
  • Neuropathology Atlas – Washington University — An extensive collection of over 33,000 annotated neuropathological images, covering a wide range of brain disorders, including neurodegenerative diseases.
  • NACC Neuropathology Forms and Coding Guidebook — A good example of how neuropathological observations, including semiquantitative assessments and staging, are translated into standardized research data.
entry.summary: How neuropathologists assess neurodegenerative changes, from semiquantitative scores and staging to quantitative methods, and why this matters for computational neuropathology.

entry.title: From the beginning: What is neuropathology and why does it matter?

link.title: From the beginning: What is neuropathology and why does it matter?

entry.content:
How I ended up in neuropathology

The brain fascinated me from the very beginning. My first approach to studying it was highly theoretical, as I studied cognitive science at the Department of Philosophy. I quickly realized, however, that the real stuff for me was happening in psychology and neurobiology.

I tried my hand at research in several different labs, developed my first (very bad) algorithm for pupil detection in videos of mice, and, thanks to an amazing internship in genomics, discovered the fascinating world of neurodegenerative diseases.

Why am I mentioning this? Because all these research experiences had one thing in common: machines collected data, and we analyzed them.

Imagine my surprise when I started my dream PhD and discovered that data collection involved looking at tissue sections and saying, “It looks moderate,” followed by “Hmm, this one looks worse, let’s call it severe.”

What do you even mean by that? 😲 What are the criteria? (Shout-out to my great former supervisor, Dr. Thal, who survived having me as a PhD student.)

It turns out that this educated judgment, a combination of experience, established criteria, and intuition, is remarkably difficult to reproduce computationally. Much of what we know about neurodegenerative diseases today comes from precisely this kind of assessment.

In my next post, I will explain why this approach works so well, despite its seemingly subjective nature. I will also argue that many aspects of neuropathology can be viewed as a highly sophisticated, biology-driven object detection problem, a perspective that could help us standardize and automate parts of the process. This is precisely why I joined Dr. Irwin’s lab. I share his vision of bringing traditional neuropathology and computational approaches together, not simply to automate existing methods, but to ask biological questions that were previously difficult or impossible to address.

By now, you have probably realized that I am not a neuropathologist. While I am not qualified to make formal neuropathological diagnoses, I am a neuroscientist and a self-proclaimed neuropathology enthusiast. This brings me to another point I would like to make throughout this blog: neuropathology is much more than a diagnostic discipline.

For those coming from other scientific backgrounds, neuropathology can seem like a rather mysterious world, with its own terminology, methods, and unwritten rules. Yet human brain tissue offers a unique opportunity to answer fundamental biological questions. I believe that making neuropathological research more accessible to scientists from different disciplines, while building on the expertise of neuropathologists, could bring new perspectives and methods to the field and open up entirely new avenues of research.

With this in mind, let us begin.

What is neuropathology?

The word neuropathology combines the Greek roots neuron (nerve), pathos (suffering or disease), and logos (study). Interestingly, the term is thought to have been coined by Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834), an English poet and philosopher, although its meaning at the time was quite different from what we understand by neuropathology today. Coleridge himself had quite a personal relationship with medicine, suffering from chronic health problems and using opium to relieve his symptoms [1].

Today, neuropathology is a subspecialty of anatomical pathology that focuses on diseases of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, but also extends to skeletal muscle and the eye [2]. The focus on disease distinguishes neuropathology from neuroanatomy, although the boundary between the two disciplines is rather thin. After all, recognizing what is abnormal requires a good understanding of what is normal.

Neuropathologists also differ from neurologists, who primarily work directly with living patients, whereas neuropathologists diagnose diseases by examining tissues and cells, often in combination with molecular analyses.

The brain, however, is a particularly difficult organ to study. Unlike many other organs, it is relatively inaccessible during life, and removing even a small piece of it can have serious consequences. As a result, much of what we know about the cellular and molecular changes occurring in the human brain during neurodegeneration comes from studying postmortem tissue.

Although neuropathology covers a wide range of conditions, from brain tumors to infections, strokes, and developmental abnormalities, neurodegenerative diseases occupy a special place within the field. While many other neurological conditions can be reliably diagnosed during life, postmortem neuropathological examination has historically been, and often remains, the gold standard for confirming the underlying causes of neurodegenerative diseases [3, 12].

For this reason, and because neurodegenerative diseases are the focus of my own research, this blog will primarily explore the changes that occur in the human brain during aging and neurodegeneration.

Where does human brain tissue come from?

Much of human neuropathological research would not be possible without brain donation, and we are extremely grateful to every wonderful person who has made this decision, as well as to their families.

Brain donations are often arranged through programs established in collaboration with neurologists and other clinicians, who inform their patients about the possibility of donating their brains after death. Donations can also be arranged by family members, subject to the relevant consent requirements. In some cases tissue is obtained through collaborations with medical examiners and forensic pathologists [4, 5].

Donated brains are collected, processed, examined, preserved, and made available to researchers through institutions called brain banks [4, 5]. Because many brain banks are associated with specialized neurological clinics, their collections often contain a relatively high proportion of individuals with neurological diseases. Obtaining well-characterized control tissue can therefore be challenging.

Interestingly, a person who had no neurological symptoms during life may still have considerable pathological changes in their brain [3, 6]. This makes donations from individuals without neurological symptoms particularly valuable, not only for understanding normal aging but also for investigating why some people are more resilient to pathological changes than others.

From brain donation to microscope slides

Once collected, the brain is typically weighed, photographed, and macroscopically examined. Visible abnormalities, such as atrophy (a reduction in tissue volume), vascular changes, infarcts, hemorrhages, and unusual anatomical features, are documented [7].

A common approach is to preserve one cerebral hemisphere in a chemical fixative, usually formalin, and freeze the other hemisphere or selected parts of it. Fixed tissue is particularly useful for microscopic examination, while frozen tissue is valuable for many molecular and biochemical analyses [4, 5, 7].

Brain tissue is extremely precious, and decisions about how to process it need to be made before we even know what research questions it might help answer in the future. Each brain bank therefore has its own protocols, designed to make the tissue useful for as many types of research as possible.

The next step is to sample specific brain regions. The brain is far from uniform, and different neurodegenerative diseases preferentially affect different regions. For example, the hippocampus is particularly important in the assessment of Alzheimer’s disease, while the substantia nigra is important in the assessment of Parkinson’s disease [3, 6].

The cerebral hemispheres are commonly cut into coronal slabs approximately one centimeter thick. Within these slabs, key anatomical landmarks are identified, and smaller pieces of tissue containing specific brain regions, known as tissue blocks, are collected [7].

In neuropathology, where something happens is often just as important as what happens.

The fixed tissue blocks are then processed and embedded in a supporting medium, most commonly paraffin wax (relatively cheap and easy to use). Using an instrument called a microtome, the tissue is cut into very, very thin sections, only a few micrometers thick, and transferred onto glass microscope slides [8].

One of the great advantages of paraffin-embedded tissue is that it can be stored and remain useful for decades, although not all molecular targets are equally well preserved [9]. This allows us to study tissue collected many years ago using technologies that did not even exist at the time of collection!

Because these very thin sections are largely transparent (with a few interesting exceptions that deserve a separate discussion), they usually need to be stained.

Conventional histological stains, such as hematoxylin and eosin, use dyes to visualize different tissue structures, while immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibodies to detect specific targets, most commonly proteins. Depending on the staining method, we can visualize individual neurons, glial cells, blood vessels, or disease-associated protein aggregates [3, 8].

However, how the tissue was collected, preserved, processed, stored, and stained can influence what we ultimately see under the microscope. These sources of variability are among the reasons why obtaining reliable and comparable quantitative measurements from histological sections remains so challenging [9, 10].

From microscope slides to digital images

Traditionally, stained tissue sections have been examined using brightfield microscopy. Neuropathologists describe the observed changes and often use semiquantitative scoring systems to assess their severity. For example, the amount of protein pathology in a particular brain region might be described as absent, mild, moderate, or severe [6, 10].

Alternatively, we can use fluorescence-based techniques, such as immunofluorescence. These techniques can facilitate quantitative measurements and allow us to visualize multiple proteins within the same tissue section, helping us investigate how different pathological changes and cell types relate to one another [11].

Increasingly, glass slides are scanned to generate high-resolution digital images, known as whole-slide images (WSI). While quantitative approaches in neuropathology have existed for decades, slide scanning allows us to perform such analyses on a much larger scale [12].

Rather than simply describing how much pathology is present, we can ask more detailed questions. How many protein aggregates are there? Do they differ in size or shape? Are they more common in particular cortical layers? Are certain types of neurons more vulnerable than others?

This is where computational neuropathology comes into play, combining traditional neuropathological knowledge with image analysis, statistics, computer vision, and machine learning [12].

This approach, however, comes with its own set of challenges, which I will explore in later posts.

Why does neuropathology matter?

By examining changes at the cellular and molecular levels, neuropathology helps us understand the biological processes underlying neurological diseases. It also teaches us about normal brain structure, how the brain ages, and how it differs between individuals.

Interestingly, two patients may present with very similar symptoms but have quite different underlying diseases. Conversely, two individuals with similar pathological changes in their brains may have experienced very different symptoms during life [3, 6].

Although we now have access to an increasing number of biomarkers that allow us to detect disease-related changes in living patients, postmortem neuropathological examination remains an important reference for establishing the underlying diagnosis. It helps us understand these seemingly contradictory observations, refine clinical diagnoses, and evaluate the biomarkers used during life [3, 4, 6, 12].

What I find particularly fascinating about neuropathology is that, despite more than a century of examining human brains under microscopes, there is still so much to discover. Even tissue collected decades ago can offer new insights when examined using new methods or approached with different questions.

In future posts, I would like to explore how we study the human brain, what our methods can and cannot tell us, and how computational approaches might help answer some of the questions that remain unresolved.

Words to use to impress a neuropathologist

  • Postmortem tissue: tissue collected after death.
  • Brain bank: an institution that collects, preserves, characterizes, and distributes human brain tissue for research.
  • Protein aggregates: abnormal accumulations of proteins that can form within or outside cells (often informally referred to as “pathology”).
  • Atrophy: a reduction in the size or volume of a tissue or organ.
  • Macroscopic examination: examination of tissue structures and abnormalities visible without a microscope.
  • Fixation: preservation of tissue, usually using chemicals, to prevent degradation and maintain its structure.
  • Coronal slab: a relatively thick slice of the brain cut in a plane that separates its front and back.
  • Tissue block: a small piece of tissue collected for further processing and examination.
  • Paraffin embedding: the process of embedding tissue in wax to provide support for cutting thin sections.
  • Microtome: an instrument used to cut very thin tissue sections.
  • Immunohistochemistry: a technique that uses antibodies to visualize specific targets within tissue sections.
  • Immunofluorescence: a technique that uses antibodies and fluorescent labels to visualize specific targets.
  • Semiquantitative scoring: assessing the extent or severity of tissue changes using ordered categories rather than direct numerical measurements.
  • Whole-slide image: a high-resolution digital image of the tissue on a microscope slide.
  • Computational neuropathology: the application of computational methods to the detection, measurement, and interpretation of neuropathological features.

Helpful resources for the curious

Brain cutting and trimming – Yasushi Iwasaki (2022)

A very good illustrated overview of brain examination, cutting, and the selection of tissue blocks for neuropathological assessment.

An Introduction to the Brain Autopsy – Vanessa Smith (2024)

A step-by-step video from the American Association of Neuropathologists’ Teaching Rounds showing brain cutting and tissue block preparation.

Neuropathology – Dimitri P. Agamanolis

A comprehensive, freely accessible, illustrated compendium of neuropathology, covering much more than neurodegenerative diseases.

WebPath: Neuropathology – University of Utah

An extensive educational collection of macroscopic and microscopic images illustrating different diseases of the nervous system.
